The Man Who Sold the War Left on Schedule

The plan to bring down the Islamic Republic was written down. It was persuasive enough to help move a US president to war in February. The people now losing their jobs over it are not the ones who sold it.

David Barnea sold it. The New York Times reported in March that Barnea, then Mossad chief, convinced Netanyahu a war could set off a rebellion inside Iran, and that he put the idea to the Trump administration during a White House visit in January. 

He left office on June 2 at the end of his term, with honors, having used his farewell address to describe toppling the regime as a legitimate objective. Netanyahu told his successor at the handover: you will remove Iran's regime from the world.

The clearing-out started underneath him. In June, incoming director Roman Gofman dismissed the deputy chief, identified in Israeli media only as A., who had run the Iran project — a billion shekels and several hundred people, granted a year earlier. 

Twenty-two years of service, five Israel Security Prizes, and a statement of deep appreciation from the Prime Minister's Office. 

On Thursday, Channel 12 reported that Gofman has now removed the head of the Mossad's intelligence directorate, in post since December, and the head of the Iran division. 

Both were among the authors of the written operational plan to topple the regime with Iran's minority groups and install a replacement leadership. 

Security sources say they had clashed with Gofman from the start, and that the departures are by mutual agreement, part of a broader reorganization.

They are probably telling the truth about the reorganization. Dagan, Cohen and Barnea each fired senior people or triggered resignations on arrival, and all three are remembered as successful directors. 

Turnover at the top of the Mossad when a new chief walks in is close to automatic. What makes this round worth reading is not that people were removed. It is which people.

The premise has not been retired. Gofman himself told Netanyahu, according to three Israeli officials speaking to CNN, that a war with Iran would produce a swift collapse of the government. 

Four months on the government is still there and Washington is negotiating with it over the nuclear file. 

Gofman considers Barnea's method to have failed, and that he is developing his own: Mossad-run social media campaigns, and the Kurds. At his swearing-in he said the heart of the Mossad lies in covert operations against its targets.

So the file stays open and the staff turns over. The officer who wrote the memo is out. The officer who ran the budget is out. The chief who sold the theory to two prime ministers' worth of political appetite and one American president finished his five years and went home. 

His successor holds the same theory, has already been wrong with it once in public, and is now hiring for a different set of local partners.

Nobody was dismissed for believing Iran could be restructured from outside. Two men were dismissed for being the ones holding it when it didn't work.
